name: Base rate fallacy
statement: Told that a test with a 5% false-positive rate flags a disease one person in a thousand has, the commonest answer from doctors is 95%, and the right one is about 2%.
meaning: Bayes's rule says a posterior probability depends on three things: how common the condition is, how often the test catches it, and how often the test fires on people who do not have it. The complaint is that people attend to the second and third and drop the first. Two families of demonstration sit under the one name and they are not the same experiment. In the diagnosis family the numbers are all given, the answer is a calculation, and the finding is a percentage of people who get it wrong. In the personality-sketch family a description is drawn from a stated mix of two professions, and the finding is that judgments barely move when the mix is reversed. That second family is the property of the representativeness heuristic, which supplies the mechanism: a description that sounds like an engineer is treated as evidence of an engineer whatever the panel contained. This entry follows the first family, where the stakes are diagnostic tests, screening programmes and forensic evidence. Neglecting the prior is one of two ways to miss the target, and the other has its own literature. Conservatism in belief revision is the finding that people underweight the likelihood term, so their posteriors move too little rather than too much. Benjamin lists underinference and base-rate neglect as separate stylized facts, and writes that the evidence for one is not in tension with the evidence for the other. The conservatism entry sets out how the sign of the error depends on the strength of the signal.

origin.note: "On the Psychology of Prediction" reported the engineer-lawyer problem, in which descriptions were said to be drawn at random from a panel of either 30 engineers and 70 lawyers or 70 engineers and 30 lawyers. The 1973 paper could not be obtained during this check, at APA PsycNET, CiteSeerX, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, the Internet Archive or four university mirrors, so every figure attributed to it here is at one remove. Chan's summary table gives its third study as 171 people, 86 in the high-engineer condition and 85 in the low, with mean judgments of 55% against 50%, t(169) = 3.23, p < .01. Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank report the same 5-point gap and add that the median judgment for the deliberately uninformative description of Dick was .50 in both groups. The gap was significant and was called small. The medical version arrived separately and is the one that travels.

evidence: The mammography problem is the canonical case. A woman of forty has a 1% chance of breast cancer, the test catches 80% of cancers, and it fires on 9.6% of women without one. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage state the Bayesian answer as 7.8%, and report that Eddy's 1982 chapter found 95 of 100 physicians putting it between 70% and 80%. Eddy's chapter was not obtained during this check, so that figure reaches this page at one remove. Casscells, Schoenberger and Graboys ran a shorter version at four Harvard Medical School teaching hospitals: a disease with a prevalence of 1 in 1,000, a false-positive rate of 5%, and a positive result. Their 1978 report is a three-page letter and could not be obtained either, at the New England Journal of Medicine, PubMed, PubMed Central, Unpaywall or Semantic Scholar. Manrai and colleagues reproduce both the question and the sample, 20 medical students, 20 house officers and 20 attending physicians, and give 11 of 60 correct, which is the 18% Gigerenzer and colleagues also quote, with 27 of 60 answering 95%. The cab problem made the point without medicine. Bar-Hillel sets out the version she credits to Kahneman and Tversky: 85% of a city's cabs are Blue, a witness right about 80% of the time identifies a Green cab, and Bayes gives 41%. Of her 52 respondents, 36% answered 80%, which was also the median, and only about 10% came near 41%. Her respondents were mostly Hebrew University applicants answering inside their entrance exams.

replication.headline: The diagnostic version repeats almost exactly across four decades and rewriting it as counts of people roughly triples the number of correct answers, while the engineer-lawyer version has now failed in two large modern samples.
replication.detail: Manrai, Bhatia, Strymish, Kohane and Jain put the Casscells question to 61 people at a Boston-area hospital, 24 of them attending physicians. Fourteen (23%) gave the correct 2%, 27 (44%) said 95%, and the median answer was 66%, which the authors note is 33 times the true value. They report the gap from Casscells as 5 percentage points, 95% CI -11% to 21%, which is no detectable change across the intervening decades. Stengård, Juslin, Hahn and van den Berg ran the classic wording on 100 online participants as a control: 9% were correct within a tolerance of 1.8% to 2.2%, and the modal answer was again 95%, at about a fifth of responses. Gigerenzer and colleagues report a training session in 2007 at which 160 gynaecologists were given a 1% prevalence, a 90% sensitivity and a 9% false-positive rate and four answer options an order of magnitude apart. Estimates ranged from 1% to 90%, most chose 81% or 90%, and 21% picked the correct 1 in 10, which the authors call slightly less than chance for a four-option question. After the same numbers were retaught as natural frequencies, 87% got it right. The format effect is the most-repeated result here. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage gave 60 paid students at the University of Salzburg 15 inference problems, each in two of four versions, scoring an answer as Bayesian only when both the process and the number were right. Probability wording produced 16% Bayesian solutions with the standard menu and 28% with the short menu. The same information written as counts produced 46% and 50%. McDowell and Jacobs pooled 226 performance estimates from 35 articles; Weber, Binder and Krauss quote them as putting performance at 24% for natural frequencies against 4% for probabilities. Bramwell, West and Salmon tested a Down's syndrome screening question on 43 pregnant women, 40 companions, 42 midwives and 41 obstetricians, 166 people analysed of the 169 randomised. Twenty-four of 166 were right. Frequencies beat percentages, 24% against 6% (χ² = 10.4, df = 1, P = 0.001), and 86% of responses were still wrong. Stengård and colleagues found the same direction and a smaller gap across 45 trials crossing five base rates, three hit rates and three false-alarm rates: mean absolute error was 18.0 with natural frequencies against 23.2 with normalised formats, on a Bayesian ANOVA with an inclusion Bayes factor of 23.2 for format, and 46 of 91 participants were fitted best by a Bayesian model against 31 of 91, p = 0.035 by Fisher's exact test. Their two symbolic conditions analysed 182 people of 189 who took part. The personality-sketch version behaves differently. Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank re-ran the engineer-lawyer problem on 97 students at the University of Constance, in cells of 24, 24, 24 and 25. Merely asserting random sampling gave a base-rate effect of 9.8 points, about twice the original 5. Letting participants draw the description from an urn themselves lifted it to 17.3 points, moving their index of base-rate use from .35 to .63, a gain the authors report as significant at p < .05. Chan, supervised by Feldman, ran a registered-report replication of the whole 1973 paper on 801 US participants from Prolific, of 1,031 who began. In its third study each participant judged one of six descriptions under one of the two panels. The base-rate manipulation produced a main effect of F(1, 789) = 102.77, p < .001, eta-squared = .081, and the description written to carry no information drew a mean of 64.27% in the high-engineer condition against 32.65% in the low, which is base-rate use rather than neglect. The report was preregistered on the Open Science Framework and passed the first round of Peer Community in Registered Reports review, and its own front matter records that data collection happened before in-principle acceptance. Toubia and colleagues put a single description, Jack, to a representative US panel in waves one and four of a four-wave study whose 2,058 completers came from 2,509 recruited. Mean judgments were 52.17% in the 30-engineer condition and 68.01% in the 70-engineer condition (t = -15.78, p < .01), and 52.39% against 70.71% in wave four (t = -19.36, p < .01). They report it as the one between-subject classic in their battery that did not replicate.

study.cite: Manrai, A. K., Bhatia, G., Strymish, J., Kohane, I. S., & Jain, S. H. (2014). Medicine's uncomfortable relationship with math: Calculating positive predictive value. JAMA Internal Medicine, 174(6), 991-993.

limits: No multi-site replication of base-rate neglect was located. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, PubMed Central, OpenAlex, arXiv, the Open Science Framework and the journals themselves turned up no Many Labs or Registered Replication Report entry for either paradigm. What the search did turn up is one registered-report replication of the engineer-lawyer problem, Chan's, run in a single laboratory, so the record is a meta-analysis, that report, one large representative survey and single-laboratory experiments. Four documents could not be obtained: Kahneman and Tversky's 1973 paper, Eddy's 1982 book chapter, the 1978 Casscells letter and the full text of Thompson and Schumann. The first three reach this page through Chan, through Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank, through Gigerenzer and Hoffrage and through Manrai and colleagues, all of whom reproduce their numbers. Operskalski and Barbey's 2016 piece in Science on risk literacy in medical decision-making sits behind a paywall and was not read, so nothing is quoted from it. The famous physician figures also rest on small samples: 60 people in 1978, 100 in Eddy's chapter, 61 in the 2014 repeat, 160 gynaecologists in one afternoon. The effect is measured almost entirely in one corner of the problem space. Stengård and colleagues make the point directly: the standard problems use base rates near zero, near-perfect hit rates and low false-alarm rates, where a Bayesian answer and base-rate neglect are far apart. Across five base rates from 0.1 to 0.9 they found the pattern generalises, but with a bimodal split, one group of participants ignoring the base rate almost entirely and another using it almost fully. Howe, Perfors, Walker, Kashima and Fay found the same shape from the other direction, asking people for whole distributions rather than single numbers. Their first experiment kept 362 of the 452 people recruited. Of those, 51.4% weighted their own stated prior at less than a tenth after seeing five chips and 17.8% weighted it almost fully, while about half also underweighted the likelihood, and no systematic relationship between the two appeared within individuals. A group average of partial neglect can describe a population in which nobody partially neglects anything.
misreadings: The strongest reading, that people ignore base rates, is the one the evidence does not carry. Koehler's review concluded that base rates are almost always used, and that the degree of use depends on task structure and representation. Gigerenzer, Hell and Blank make the same case with a manipulation: base-rate use rose when random sampling could be watched rather than asserted. Kahneman and Tversky replied that the critique misrepresents their position, and that judgments of frequency carry large and systematic biases of their own. The second error is treating natural frequencies as a general fix. Weber, Binder and Krauss found that about 49% of people handed a frequency version converted it back into probabilities and calculated with those, and they open by noting that three-quarters of the people in McDowell and Jacobs's meta-analysis got a frequency version wrong. Chapman and Liu gave 346 students the Lipkus numeracy scale and split them at the median. On the medical scenario, correct answers went from 1% to 27% with frequencies among the 190 high scorers and from 0% to 7% among the 156 low scorers, a format-by-numeracy interaction of χ²(1) = 13.29, p = .0003. Bramwell's data point the same way: the format gain was statistically reliable only among obstetricians, who went from 1 of 21 correct with percentages to 13 of 20 with frequencies, while midwives got none right in either arm. The reformulation helps the people who could already have done the arithmetic. The third error is reading the medical result as a fact about doctors. Obstetricians were the best of Bramwell's four groups, at 34%, or 14 of 41, ahead of companions at 15% and pregnant women at 9%, which says more about the question than about the professions. That paper's own abstract puts the obstetricians at 43% where its table puts them at 34%, and the table is the figure used here. The courtroom version of the same mistake has its own name. Thompson and Schumann called it the prosecutor's fallacy: treating the chance of a forensic match given innocence as the chance of innocence given a match. Their full text could not be obtained at Springer, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar or the authors' pages, so this page quotes no figures from it. Its abstract reports two experiments on undergraduates, the first finding that incidence rates given as conditional probabilities promoted errors favouring the prosecution while percentages produced more errors favouring the defence, and the second finding that most people failed to spot the error in one or both of two fallacious arguments.
